page: Microsoft Azure E4ds_v6 is a memory-optimized virtual machine belonging to the Edsv6 family. It is powered by an Intel Xeon 8573C processor running at 4.2 GHz, featuring 4 vCPUs mapped to 2 physical cores with Hyper-Threading. The instance is equipped with 32.0 GB of RAM, providing a high memory-to-vCPU ratio of 8.0 GB per core. It includes 236 GB of local storage and supports Premium Storage.

In benchmark evaluations, the E4ds_v6 demonstrates strong single-core performance, as evidenced by its Geekbench single-core score of 2156.0 and single-threaded gzip compression rate of 31.35 GB/sec. However, multi-core scaling presents a tradeoff; the multi-core stress-ng performance and multi-threaded bzip3 decompression fall into the lower 25% percentile. Memory read bandwidth is also relatively low, with uncached large-block reads measuring 36.24 GB/sec, though write bandwidth remains average at 25.93 GB/sec.

Given its high memory density relative to the 4 vCPU count, this server offers qualitative cost efficiency for workloads that require substantial memory footprints without demanding massive parallel processing power. The inclusion of 236 GB of local storage makes it suitable for database operations, caching layers, and memory-intensive applications such as light relational databases, text processing, and web serving, while avoiding the overhead of larger compute-heavy instances.
description: The Microsoft Azure E4ds_v6 is an x86_64 memory-optimized virtual machine from the Edsv6 family, running on Microsoft Hyper-V. It features 4 dedicated vCPUs powered by an Intel Xeon 8573C processor clocked at 4.2 GHz, paired with 32.0 GB of RAM and 236 GB of local storage. This configuration yields a high memory-to-vCPU ratio of 8.0 GB per core. Benchmark data reveals strong single-core capabilities, highlighted by a Geekbench single-core score of 2156.0 and efficient single-threaded text and gzip processing. Conversely, multi-core scaling and read memory bandwidth are weaker, positioning this instance as a specialized option for memory-bound tasks rather than highly parallel compute workloads. It is well-suited for database operations, memory caching, and web serving where memory capacity is prioritized over high core counts.
